name: DS-Agent: Automated Data Science by Empowering Large Language Models with Case-Based Reasoning
venue: ICML 2024 (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR vol. 235, pp. 16813-16848); preprint arXiv:2402.17453 (cs.LG)
authors_affiliation: Siyuan Guo, Cheng Deng, Ying Wen, Hechang Chen, Yi Chang, Jun Wang. Lead author Siyuan Guo is a PhD student at Jilin University, China; co-authors Hechang Chen and Yi Chang are also at Jilin University; Jun Wang is a Professor of Computer Science at University College London (UCL). Cheng Deng and Ying Wen are associated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University. [uncertain] (exact per-author affiliation mapping for Deng/Wen not explicitly tabulated in the open PDF).
task_domain: code / decision-making: LLM-agent automated data science (automated machine learning) - comprehending a task description, then building, training, and validating the best-fit ML model via generated and executed Python code. Spans three data modalities (text, time series, tabular) and two ML task types (regression, classification).
problem_setting: Interactive, single-agent, closed-loop automated data science. A task is a tuple (task description tau, D_train, D_valid, D_test, evaluation metric M); the agent comprehends tau, generates code to train an ML model on D_train, evaluates on D_valid via M, and is scored on D_test. Two distinct stages: (1) a high-resource Development stage that runs a full CBR automatic iteration pipeline with code execution feedback (multiple iterations per task, T=5); (2) a low-resource Deployment stage that uses a simplified one-shot CBR (retrieve one past successful case, adapt, generate code directly, no execution loop). 30 tasks total (12 development, 18 deployment); datasets mostly released after Sep 2021 to avoid pretraining contamination. No gradient finetuning of the LLM - the only 'learning' is retaining successful cases into the case bank. Supervision: expert knowledge cases crawled from Kaggle (winners' technical reports + top public-leaderboard code summarized by GPT-3.5).
what_is_retrieved: cases: in the development stage, human-insight cases from a Kaggle-derived case bank C (cleaned winner technical reports + GPT-3.5-summarized textual solution insights from top public code) plus retained successful (task description, Python script) solution cases; in the deployment stage, past successful (tau_0, s_0) solution-code case pairs from the agent experience case bank B.
retrieval_grounding: HYBRID: an initially offline-induced static human-insight case bank C crawled from Kaggle, which also GROWS at test time (development stage retains new successful cases into both C and the agent case bank B). Deployment retrieves from the grown agent case bank B (which was filled during development; frozen at deployment time).
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Two-level objective. The dense retriever returns a fixed top-k (k=5) candidate set by cosine similarity (a fixed top-k ranking). The ReviseRanker (LLM) then re-orders these k cases and selects a single best case for reuse. The reuse process is centered on adapting ONE example case; ablation shows adding more than one case in context hurts performance, so effectively the objective is a precision-driven single-case selection rather than a completeness/minimal-set objective.
retrieval_unit: case (problem-solution): a (task description, solution) pair. In the development case bank these are human-insight cases (textual expert solution insights extracted from Kaggle reports/code) and retained (task, Python script) pairs; in deployment they are (task description, successful Python solution code) pairs. Effectively a full-solution/case unit expressed as textual insight or executable code.
index_source: Hybrid construction: offline-induced human-insight case bank C crawled from 12 recently-completed Kaggle competitions (4 per modality; top-10 winner technical reports + top-10 public-leaderboard Jupyter notebooks summarized into textual insights by GPT-3.5). The store then grows online during the development stage as successful solution cases are retained into both C and the agent experience case bank B. Deployment retrieves from B (induced during development, then fixed).
index_structure_topology: Flat vector index keyed by task-description embeddings (cosine similarity over llm-embedder embeddings). No graph or hierarchical topology is described; cases are organized as a flat case bank (the human insight bank C and the agent experience bank B).
retriever_type: dense (off-the-shelf): a pretrained embedding model (llm-embedder, Zhang et al. 2023b) computes embeddings and cosine similarity sim(tau,c)=cos(E(tau),E(c)) for top-k retrieval, followed by an LLM-as-reranker (ReviseRank) stage that uses the LLM to re-order candidates - so the overall pipeline is dense-retriever + LLM-as-reranker (a form of hybrid dense + generative reranking).
retriever_learning_signal: none for the dense retriever (off-the-shelf llm-embedder, not trained on task feedback). The ReviseRank stage is LM-feedback / execution-feedback driven but not gradient-trained: the paper explicitly notes that finetuning the retriever on execution feedback is too expensive (requires code execution), so instead the LLM estimates each candidate case's utility conditioned on the prior iteration's execution feedback l^{t-1} and revises the ranking via prompting (zero-shot LLM permutation generation). So the selection signal is downstream-task / execution-effectiveness, realized through an LLM reranker rather than a trained retriever.
query_construction: Raw task description tau is the retrieval key/query for the dense retriever. For ReviseRank, the query is the task description tau plus the previous iteration's execution feedback l^{t-1} (initialized empty), used by the LLM to estimate per-case utility and re-rank. No synthetic query expansion or decomposition.
query_granularity: task-level for the dense retrieval (one cosine-similarity retrieval at the task level), then iteration/trajectory-level for ReviseRank: the case selection is refined once per development iteration step (t=1..5) conditioned on the latest execution feedback. Deployment is purely task-level (single retrieval, no loop).
when_to_retrieve: Development: iterative - dense top-k retrieval at the start, then per-iteration LLM ReviseRank re-selection within the T=5 iteration loop driven by execution feedback (a Revise loop). Deployment: one-shot - a single retrieval of the most similar past case, no iteration.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Fixed schedule tied to the CBR iteration loop. Initial dense retrieval is triggered once at the start of a task. The ReviseRank re-selection is triggered each iteration step by the arrival of new execution feedback l^{t-1} (experiment log produced after code execution and debugging); the loop runs for a predetermined maximum number of iteration steps (T=5) rather than via an uncertainty/confidence trigger.
reranking: Yes - ReviseRank: an LLM-as-reranker (instruction-prompted, inspired by Sun et al. 2023 RankGPT-style listwise relevance ranking) that takes the top-k candidates with identifiers ([1],[2],...), the task tau, and the prior execution feedback l^{t-1}, and generates a descending utility permutation (e.g. [2]>[1]>[3]); the top-ranked case is selected for reuse. This is execution-feedback-aware listwise reranking.
retrieved_context_refinement: Rerank (ReviseRank re-orders the top-k candidates conditioned on execution feedback and keeps only the single top-ranked case for reuse). At case-bank-construction time, raw Kaggle code is also distilled by GPT-3.5 into textual solution insights (a content-preparation step). No distractor-filtering, compression, or decompose-then-recompose is applied to retrieved items beyond selecting one case.
how_retrieved_used: prompt augmentation + case adaptation (case reuse): the selected top-ranked case is given to the Planner (development) or Adapter (deployment), which analyzes the case's human insights / solution code and adapts/reuses it to produce a new experiment plan y^t (development) or directly generate the solution Python code s (deployment). The plan is then executed; execution feedback drives the next revision.
planning_integration: retrieve-then-plan inside an iterative CBR loop. Development pipeline per step: Retrieve (dense top-k) -> ReviseRank (LLM re-rank using feedback) -> Reuse (Planner adapts the chosen case into an experiment plan y^t) -> Execute (Programmer writes Python, runs it, Debugger fixes bugs Reflexion-style, Logger summarizes feedback l^t) -> Retain (archive improved solutions) -> loop back to ReviseRank. Deployment: single retrieve-then-adapt-then-generate-code, no loop. Planning and retrieval are tightly interleaved at the per-iteration level in development.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-iteration (per experiment-plan revision within a task). Retrieval/reranking is woven in once per CBR iteration step (T=5 steps), each tied to one plan-generate-execute-feedback cycle; not per-CoT-token or per-tool-call. Deployment is per-answer (single shot).
retrieved_item_representation: Mixed: in the development human-insight bank, items are distilled free-text strategy/insight (cleaned technical reports and GPT-3.5-summarized textual solutions describing model architecture, hyper-parameters, objective, tricks); retained solution cases and deployment cases are executable Python programs paired with task descriptions. So injected items range from distilled strategy/guideline text to executable program/skill code.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: distilled strategy/insight (textual expert solutions summarizing design choices, architectures, hyper-parameters, tricks) for human-insight cases, and reusable procedural solution (executable Python code) for retained/deployment cases. The ablation explicitly contrasts learning from a homogeneous case (example task + one of its solutions) vs heterogeneous textual human insights, finding the homogeneous (concrete solution) case more effective in deployment.
noise_robustness_mechanism: (1) ReviseRank uses execution feedback to discard misleading candidates and promote the empirically-useful case, mitigating retrieval noise from pure similarity. (2) The reuse process is restricted to a single best case - the paper shows adding extra cases injects interference/noise and degrades performance, so limiting k-in-context to 1 is itself a noise-control choice. (3) Retain only archives solutions with improved test performance, keeping the case bank high-quality. (4) Debugger (Reflexion-style self-reflection on execution errors) corrects buggy generated code before feedback is logged.
memory_type: episodic / skill-library: two case banks - a human-insight case bank C (expert knowledge) and an agent experience case bank B that stores successful (task, solution-code) cases retained during development for reuse in deployment.
write_back: Yes. At each development iteration's Retain step, if the trained model achieves improved test performance, DS-Agent archives the task description tau and its Python script s into BOTH the human-insight case bank C and the agent experience case bank B for future reuse.
online_growth: Partially. During the development stage the case banks grow at test/run time as successful cases are retained. The agent case bank B used in the deployment stage is grown during development and then fixed (frozen) for deployment; deployment itself does not write new cases back.
write_back_trigger: on-success only, gated by performance improvement: a case (tau, s) is retained into C and B only when the trained ML model shows improved performance on the test set at the end of an iteration step. Failed or non-improving solutions are not stored as cases. (Within-iteration debugging from failures occurs but is not persisted as a stored case.)
failure_experience_usage: Success-only for memory: only performance-improving solutions are retained as reusable cases. Failures/errors are handled transiently within an iteration - the Debugger reflects on execution errors (Reflexion-inspired) and the ReviseRanker uses the execution feedback log (which can reflect poor results) to re-select cases - but negative/failure cases are not stored in the case bank as retrievable contrastive items.
memory_evolution_update: append-only with a quality gate: new successful cases are appended to C and B when they improve performance; the paper does not describe dedup-merge, delta-update, refine-overwrite, or forgetting/pruning of already-stored cases.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No. The dense retriever is off-the-shelf top-k cosine similarity (not RL/value-optimized). The ReviseRank re-selection is an LLM prompting policy conditioned on execution feedback, but it is not a trained/RL-optimized retrieval policy (the paper explicitly avoids finetuning the retriever due to the cost of execution feedback).
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No. Single-agent (multi-role: Retriever, ReviseRanker, Planner, Programmer, Debugger, Logger, Adapter are sub-modules of one DS-Agent system, not independent collaborating agents) with private case banks. No cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing is described, though knowledge does transfer across the two stages (development cases reused in deployment).
benchmarks: A purpose-built suite of 30 data science tasks (12 development: FB, AR, TE, CP, ETT, ILI, HW, EC, MCS, WBY, ST, ES; 18 deployment: JS, HR, BPP, WR, DAG, BQ, TFC, WTH, ELE, SRC, UGL, HB, CA, CS, MH, SS, CO, SD), spanning text/time-series/tabular modalities and regression/classification, with metrics including accuracy, AUROC, NLL, MCRMSE, MSE, RMLSE, MAE, RMSE, MedAE. Built on top of the MLAgentBench framework. Human-insight cases crawled from 12 recently-completed Kaggle competitions.
benchmark_family: Automated data science / AutoML over Kaggle-style ML tasks (code + decision-making); built on the MLAgentBench (Huang et al. 2023) framework. Not one of the standard QA/web/embodied/tool/SWE-bench families - it is a custom Kaggle-derived data-science benchmark.
baselines: Development stage: ResearchAgent (Huang et al. 2023, the MLAgentBench SOTA language agent for ML research tasks), on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Deployment stage: Zero-shot (direct prompting) and One-shot (a random case from the agent case bank in context), each on GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and the open-source Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1. Ablations: DS-Agent w/o ReviseRank (= a RAG-based LLM agent) and DS-Agent w/o CBR.
key_metrics: Development: success rate (bug-free model build within a fixed number of steps) and mean rank / best rank w.r.t. task-specific metrics. Deployment: one-pass rate (build a working ML model in a single trial) and mean rank. Resource cost: USD per run.
headline_result: DS-Agent with GPT-4 achieves a 100% success rate in the development stage and a near-100% (GPT-3.5: 85%) one-pass rate in deployment, with a 36% average one-pass-rate improvement across alternative LLMs in deployment; it achieves the best rank in both stages, costing $1.60 per run (development) and $0.13 per run (deployment) with GPT-4 (deployment GPT-4 single run $0.1350, GPT-3.5 $0.0045 - over 90% cheaper than development).
ablations: (1) w/o ReviseRank (= RAG-based agent using the top-1 similarity case without feedback-driven re-ranking): average best rank degrades from 2.08 to 2.58 on 12 development tasks (GPT-4), showing feedback-aware reranking matters. (2) w/o CBR (prompt LLM to plan without human insights): worst, average best rank 3.41, confirming the Kaggle expert-knowledge cases are the main driver. (3) Deployment: learning from past successful (homogeneous) cases vs textual human insights (heterogeneous) - homogeneous solution cases win on nearly all tasks. (4) Hyper-parameter on number of in-context example cases: best with a single case; performance declines rapidly as more cases are added (extra cases inject interference). (5) Performance improves monotonically with CBR iteration steps (T) for both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
evaluation_decoupling: No. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are not reported. Evaluation is end-to-end (success rate, one-pass rate, mean/best rank on ML task metrics); the value of the retrieval/reranking components is shown via ablations rather than standalone retrieval metrics.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Mostly outcome (final ML model performance via mean/best rank; build success/one-pass rate). Some process insight is provided: the success/one-pass rate captures whether the pipeline can build a bug-free model (intermediate process quality), and the performance-vs-iteration-step curve shows step-wise improvement, but no formal reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Strong cost emphasis. Development with GPT-4 costs $1.60 per run; deployment $0.13 (GPT-4) / $0.0045 (GPT-3.5) per run - over 90% cheaper than development, by design (deployment drops the iteration loop and uses a single retrieved case for direct code generation). Hyper-parameters: T=5 iterations and k=5 retrieved candidates, n_debug=5 debugging attempts in development. The two-stage split (expensive exploration once, cheap reuse many times) is the core efficiency lever; deployment runs even on open-source Mixtral-8x7B.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Fixed-then-pruned: dense retrieval returns k=5 candidates, ReviseRank re-ranks them, and exactly ONE top case is injected for reuse (in both stages). The single-case budget is deliberate - the hyper-parameter study shows that injecting more than one case in context degrades performance, so selection count is effectively capped at 1 case in the prompt.
benchmark_construction_and_size: 30 human-curated data science tasks (12 development + 18 deployment) across 3 modalities (text, time series, tabular) and 2 task types (regression, classification); each task has a natural-language description, train/valid/test split, a random-guess baseline script, and a task-specific metric. Datasets sourced from varied platforms and mostly released after Sep 2021 to avoid LLM pretraining contamination; answers are verifiable via the task-specific evaluation metric on a held-out test set. Built on MLAgentBench. Best system (DS-Agent + GPT-4) attains 100% development success and best rank, indicating headroom remains on harder text/time-series tasks vs easy tabular tasks.
builds_on: Case-Based Reasoning (Aamodt & Plaza 1994; Kolodner 1992; Watson & Marir 1994); the MLAgentBench / ResearchAgent framework (Huang et al. 2023) it is implemented on top of and compared against; Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) for the self-reflective Debugger; RankGPT-style LLM relevance ranking (Sun et al. 2023) for ReviseRank; llm-embedder (Zhang et al. 2023b) as the dense embedding retriever; RAG / in-context example selection (Lewis et al. 2020; Rubin et al. 2022) as the conceptual retrieval baseline.
contrasts_with: RAG-based LLMs (formalized as retrieve-then-generate with a single latent retrieved case and NO feedback-driven case adjustment or retain step - DS-Agent's w/o ReviseRank ablation is exactly a RAG agent); plain LLM planning without expert cases (w/o CBR ablation); ResearchAgent (high reasoning/coding demand, no CBR); AutoML techniques (HPO/NAS search-based, contrasted in Appendix C as lacking LLM flexibility and case reuse); Zero-shot / One-shot (random case) prompting baselines; complementary-but-distinct concurrent work Data Interpreter (Hong et al. 2024a).
lineage: Group D (case-based planning / experience-grounded LLM planners). DS-Agent is a canonical, explicitly CBR-grounded instantiation of the full 4R cycle (Retrieve-Reuse-Revise-Retain) for ML experiment-plan generation, sitting in the lineage of CBR-augmented LLM agents and growing-memory experience planners, and explicitly positioned as a generalization of RAG (which lacks Revise + Retain).
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve: yes (dense top-k + LLM ReviseRank), Reuse: yes (Planner/Adapter adapts the chosen case into an experiment plan / code), Revise: yes (execution-feedback-driven Revise loop iteratively re-ranks cases and revises the plan over T iterations), Retain: yes (improved successful cases archived into both case banks C and B)]. All four canonical CBR phases are explicitly implemented in the development stage; deployment uses a simplified Retrieve+Reuse subset.
explicit_cbr_grounding: True. The paper explicitly frames itself as case-based reasoning, names the method as integrating CBR into LLMs, and cites the canonical CBR literature including Aamodt & Plaza (1994), Kolodner (1992), and Watson & Marir (1994); it formally contrasts CBR-based LLMs against RAG-based LLMs (the defining feedback/revise/retain distinction).
tool_document_engineering: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method). The closest analogue is case-document engineering: raw Kaggle winner code is summarized by GPT-3.5 into distilled textual solution insights, and technical reports are cleaned, before being embedded and indexed in the case bank.
index_content_separation: N/A / not explicitly separated. Cases (insight text or code) are embedded by task description and the full case content is loaded into context on retrieval; no separate lightweight-index-then-heavy-content (progressive disclosure) scheme is described.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: N/A. Not a tool/API-retrieval system; no RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling tool index. The agent interacts with the environment via Python code execution within the MLAgentBench framework, not a tool registry.
tool_dependency_awareness: N/A (no tool/API retrieval; no inter-tool dependency modeling).
adaptation_mechanism: execution-feedback-driven revision (development) plus LLM-prompted adaptation: the Planner reuses the selected case to draft an experiment plan, the plan is executed, and the resulting execution feedback drives both the next-iteration ReviseRank case re-selection and the plan revision (Revise loop). In deployment, an Adapter performs LLM-prompted adaptation of a single retrieved past solution case to the new task to directly generate code (no execution loop).
